title: IF JESUS IS REALLY GOD, WHY DID HE SAY, “THE FATHER IS GREATER THAN I”?
paragraphs: IF JESUS IS REALLY GOD, WHY DID HE SAY, “THE FATHER IS GREATER THAN I”?
The One Sentence That Seems to Contradict Christ’s Divinity—Until You Discover What Jesus Gave Up, What He Never Stopped Being, and Why He Went to the Cross for You.
There is a question that has shaken the faith of some Christians, fueled centuries of theological arguments, and left countless people wondering whether they have misunderstood Jesus all along.
And the unsettling part?
The question comes from Jesus’ own mouth.
“If ye loved me, ye would rejoice, because I said, I go unto the Father: for my Father is greater than I.” — John 14:28, KJV
Read that last sentence again.
“My Father is greater than I.”
Greater?
But haven't Christians been taught that Jesus is God?
Doesn't the Bible say that the Word was God?
If Jesus is fully divine, why would He describe the Father as greater than Himself?
Was Jesus admitting that He was somehow less than God? Was He merely a powerful messenger? A created being? Someone beneath the Father in His very nature?
Or is there something extraordinary happening in this passage that we cannot see until we understand what Jesus was doing when He spoke those words?
Because this is not merely an argument about ancient Greek vocabulary.

This question takes us straight into the mystery of the incarnation, the humility of the Son of God, the agony of Calvary, and the astonishing truth that the One who possesses divine glory willingly entered our suffering.
And somewhere in that truth is a message for the person who has spent years believing that being important means never having to humble yourself.
Stay with this.
Because before we finish, the words “the Father is greater than I” may no longer sound like a threat to your faith.
They may become one of the most beautiful reminders of what Jesus willingly endured to save you.
Imagine the upper room.
The atmosphere is heavy.
Jesus knows that betrayal is approaching. He knows that His disciples will scatter. He knows the cross is waiting.
The men around Him do not fully understand what is coming.
They have left their livelihoods to follow Him. They have watched Him open blind eyes, command storms, forgive sins, and call the dead back to life.
They believe in Him.
But now He is talking about leaving.
And their hearts are troubled.
Jesus tells them:
“Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me.” — John 14:1, KJV
Notice that.
Jesus does not tell His disciples to trust God instead of trusting Him.
He calls them to trust in God and in Himself.
Then He promises to prepare a place for them. He speaks of going to the Father. He promises the coming of the Holy Spirit.
And in the middle of comforting frightened disciples, He says something that people would later isolate from the conversation and use as an argument against His deity.
“The Father is greater than I.”
But here is where we must be careful.
A verse removed from its context can appear to say something the passage itself never intended.
Jesus was not delivering a lecture about being a lesser god.
He was comforting His disciples about His departure.
He was speaking as the eternal Son who had entered the world in genuine human flesh, taken the form of a servant, and was preparing to return to the glory of the Father.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.
And to understand why, we need to go somewhere unexpected.
Not first to the manger.
Not even to the cross.
We need to go back before Bethlehem existed.
Before Abraham.
Before the first sunrise.
Before creation itself.
John opens his Gospel with these astonishing words:
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” — John 1:1, KJV
The original Greek reads:
Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.
Transliteration:
En archē ēn ho logos, kai ho logos ēn pros ton theon, kai theos ēn ho logos.
The final phrase is crucial:
καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος
Kai theos ēn ho logos.
“And the Word was God.”
John is making two truths clear simultaneously.
The Word was with God, indicating personal distinction.
And the Word was God, affirming His deity.
The Word is not identical to the Father as a person, yet He truly possesses the divine nature.
Some object that the Greek word theos in the final clause lacks the definite article and therefore should mean “a god.”
But Greek grammar does not work that simply.

The absence of the article does not automatically make a noun indefinite. In this construction, theos stands before the verb and describes what the Word is by nature. The wording distinguishes the Word from the person identified as ton theon while affirming His deity.
John's meaning is reinforced by what he writes next:
Think about the force of those words.
Everything that came into existence came into existence through the Word.
And apart from Him, nothing that was made was made.
John does not place the Word among the things created.
He places Him on the Creator's side of the distinction between Creator and creation.
Then, in verse 14, comes the sentence that changes everything:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us...” — John 1:14, KJV
The Greek says:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
Not that the Word stopped being divine.
Not that God transformed into a mere human and ceased to be God.
The eternal Word became truly human.
This is the incarnation.
And it is impossible to understand John 14:28 properly without understanding John 1:14.
The One who became flesh did not cease to be what He eternally was. He took on what He had not previously possessed: a genuine human nature.
He entered a world of hunger, exhaustion, rejection, grief, temptation, suffering, and death.
The Creator entered His creation.
The eternal Son experienced human life.
The One through whom all things were made allowed Himself to be carried in human arms.
And eventually, He allowed human hands to nail Him to a cross.
Not because He had lost His deity.
But because He had come to redeem sinners.
Now listen carefully, because this is where another passage opens the mystery even further.
The apostle Paul writes:
Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God:
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men.” — Philippians 2:5–7, KJV
The original Greek contains a phrase that deserves serious attention:
ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ ὑπάρχων
En morphē theou hyparchōn.
“Existing in the form of God.”
The word morphē refers here to a form or condition expressive of what someone truly is. Paul's parallel between the “form of God” and the “form of a servant” is essential to his argument.
Jesus did not merely appear divine.
Paul begins with Christ's divine status and then describes His astonishing humiliation.
But the next phrase has sometimes been misunderstood:
ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν
Heauton ekenōsen.
Literally, “He emptied Himself.”
This is where the Greek verb kenoō gives us the theological term kenosis, meaning emptying.
And this raises a critical question.
What exactly did Jesus empty Himself of?
Did He surrender His deity?
Did He cease to be omnipotent?
Did He stop being God?
No.
Paul does not say that Jesus emptied Himself of His divine nature.
He explains the emptying through what follows: Christ took the form of a servant and entered genuine human existence.
His emptying was not the abandonment of deity but the astonishing humility of taking the servant's place.
He did not become less than divine in His nature.
He became truly human without ceasing to be divine.
He did not stop being the eternal Son.
He willingly embraced the lowliness and suffering of human life.
And that is why the language of “greater” in John 14:28 must be understood carefully.
The Greek word Jesus uses is:
μείζων
Meizōn.
It means “greater.”
It is a comparative word that can refer to greatness in different respects, including position, status, or authority.
The word by itself does not tell us that one person possesses a superior divine nature.
Context determines what kind of greatness is being discussed.
Within John's Gospel, Jesus speaks as the Son sent by the Father, carrying out the Father's will, and moving toward His return to the Father's glory.
The Father is greater in relation to the Son's incarnate mission and humbled condition. The Son is not thereby declared inferior in divine essence.

There is also a real distinction between the Father and the Son, including the Son's relationship to the Father and His willing obedience in the work of redemption. Christian theology must not erase that distinction.
Yet distinction of persons and order in the saving mission do not require inequality of divine nature.
This is why historic Trinitarian Christianity confesses one God in three distinct persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Not three gods.
Not one person wearing three different masks.
And not a supreme God who created a lesser divine being named Jesus.
The Father is God.
The Son is God.
The Holy Spirit is God.
They are personally distinct, yet share the one undivided divine being.
The mystery is profound, but the confession is not built upon John 1:1 alone.
Listen to Jesus elsewhere in John's Gospel:
“I and my Father are one.” — John 10:30, KJV
The Greek reads:
ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν
Egō kai ho patēr hen esmen.
The word hen, meaning “one,” is neuter, not masculine.
Jesus is not saying that He and the Father are the same person.
The plural verb “we are” preserves their personal distinction.

In context, Jesus speaks of His power to preserve His sheep and the Father's power to preserve them. The declaration of oneness is therefore bound to their unity in divine action, and John's broader Gospel supports the confession of their shared deity.
Notice what happens immediately afterward.
His opponents pick up stones.
They understand His words as making a claim that, in their judgment, constitutes blasphemy.
And Jesus does not respond by declaring Himself merely a created angel.
Instead, He continues speaking of His unique relationship with the Father.
Elsewhere He says:
“Before Abraham was, I am.” — John 8:58, KJV
The Greek is striking:
πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι ἐγὼ εἰμί
Prin Abraam genesthai egō eimi.
Before Abraham came into existence, Jesus says, “I am.”
The wording contrasts Abraham's coming into being with Jesus' extraordinary claim about Himself.
In the context of John's Gospel, it contributes to the revelation of His preexistence and divine identity.

There is also a meaningful connection with the divine self-revelation in Exodus, though we should not pretend that every Greek occurrence of egō eimi automatically carries the full meaning of God's name.
Sound interpretation respects both the words and their setting.
And John does not leave us guessing about where his Gospel is leading.
After the resurrection, Thomas sees the risen Jesus and cries:
“My Lord and my God.” — John 20:28, KJV
The Greek says:
Ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου
Ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou.
“My Lord and my God.”
Thomas addresses Jesus directly.
And Jesus does not rebuke him for calling Him God.
Instead, He speaks of the blessedness of those who will believe without seeing.
That matters.
Because the same Gospel that records Jesus saying “the Father is greater than I” also records Thomas calling Jesus “my God.”
If we allow John to interpret John, we cannot casually discard one passage to preserve another.
We must hold both truths together.
Jesus is truly God.
Jesus is truly man.
The Son is distinct from the Father.
And in His earthly mission, the incarnate Son willingly obeyed the Father.
This is not a contradiction.
It is the heart of the incarnation.
But there is another detail in John 14:28 that is often overlooked.
Jesus says:
“If ye loved me, ye would rejoice...”
Why would His disciples rejoice that He was going to the Father?
Because His departure was not a defeat.
His humiliation was moving toward its appointed completion.
His death and resurrection would accomplish redemption, and His return to the Father would mean the glorification of the incarnate Son.
Earlier, Jesus had prayed:
“And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.” — John 17:5, KJV
Before the world was.
Before creation.
Before Bethlehem.
Jesus speaks of glory He already shared with the Father.
He is not asking to become divine for the first time.
He is speaking of the glory that was His before the world existed, now to be manifested in the completion of His saving mission.
The Father is greater than the Son in the Son's humbled earthly condition, but the Son's eternal divine identity has not disappeared.
And the story does not end with humiliation.
Paul continues:
“And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:
That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth;
And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” — Philippians 2:8–11, KJV
There is something breathtaking here.
The One who stooped to the lowest place is exalted.
The One who accepted the servant's condition is confessed as Lord.
And Paul is drawing upon language from Isaiah 45:23, where the LORD declares that every knee will bow and every tongue will swear allegiance.
In the Hebrew Scriptures, Isaiah's declaration belongs to the one true God.
The Hebrew includes the words:
כִּי־לִי תִּכְרַע כָּל־בֶּרֶךְ
Ki li tikhra kol berekh.
“To me every knee shall bow.”
Paul applies this universal confession to Jesus Christ, while explicitly declaring that it brings glory to God the Father.
This is not a picture of a rival deity stealing the Father's honor.
It is a picture of the Father being glorified through the universal acknowledgment of the Son.
And now we have reached the point where this theological question becomes painfully personal.
Because Philippians 2 was not originally written merely to settle arguments about Christology.
Paul begins with a command:
“Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus.”
He is speaking to believers about humility.
About selfish ambition.
About pride.
About considering others.
About the kind of heart that should exist among people who belong to Jesus.
And then he points to the Son of God.
Think about the contrast.
We are often desperate to be recognized.
Jesus willingly embraced humiliation.
We want people to notice our importance.
Jesus washed His disciples' feet.
We struggle to apologize because admitting wrong feels like losing.
Jesus, who committed no sin, accepted shame He did not deserve.
We want to defend our reputation at any cost.
Jesus endured mockery, false accusation, and crucifixion to accomplish the Father's saving purpose.
And perhaps that is where this passage begins to confront us.
Not because we have misunderstood a Greek verb.
But because we have misunderstood greatness.
We have spent so much of our lives believing that greatness means being above other people.
Being untouchable.
Being admired.
Being the one who never has to bend.
Yet the eternal Son, who had every right to divine glory, took the form of a servant.
The One who had nothing to prove humbled Himself for people who had nothing to boast about.
And some of us still cannot bring ourselves to say, “I was wrong.”
Some of us would rather lose a relationship than surrender our pride.
Some of us know how to defend the doctrine of Christ's deity while refusing to imitate the humility of Christ's heart.
We can explain the Trinity and still treat people cruelly.
We can quote Philippians 2 and still hunger for applause.
We can win an argument about Jesus and walk away behaving nothing like Him.
That should disturb us.
Because biblical truth is not given merely to make us better debaters.
It is given to lead us into worship, repentance, faith, and transformed living.
And before anyone misunderstands, humility does not mean pretending evil is good, remaining in abuse, or refusing to speak truth.
Jesus was humble without being dishonest.
He was gentle without surrendering righteousness.
He served without ceasing to be Lord.
His humility was holy strength directed toward the Father's will.
And that is what makes the cross so overwhelming.
Jesus was not a helpless victim trapped by circumstances beyond His control.
He willingly laid down His life.
He said:
“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.” — John 10:18, KJV
He knew what was coming.
He knew the betrayal.
He knew the abandonment.
He knew the agony.
And He went forward.
For sinners.
For the proud.
For the ashamed.
For those who have tried to cover their guilt with religious appearances.
For people who know what it means to smile in public while privately wondering whether God could still forgive them.
Perhaps that is you.
Perhaps you have been reading about Greek grammar while carrying something much heavier than a theological question.
A failure you have never confessed.
A habit you keep returning to.
A relationship damaged by your pride.
A secret that makes you afraid of being fully known.
And somewhere beneath all your religious language is a question you have not dared to say aloud:
“If Jesus really knew everything about me, would He still want me?”
Here is what the Gospel declares.
He does know the truth about sinners.
And He came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we earned a second chance.
Not after we became impressive enough to deserve mercy.
While we were still sinners.
The eternal Son entered our humanity, lived in perfect obedience, bore our sins at the cross, and rose from the dead.
His sacrifice is not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
It is the foundation of forgiveness and the call to a new life.
Grace does not tell us that sin is harmless.
Grace tells us that sin is so serious that Christ died to save us from it—and that God's mercy is so great that sinners can be forgiven through Him.
This is where scandal meets grace.
The scandal of our rebellion.
The scandal of our hypocrisy.
The scandal of our desperate attempts to save ourselves.
And then the grace of Jesus Christ.
Not a grace that denies the truth.
A grace that confronts our sin, offers forgiveness, and transforms those who come to Him in repentance and faith.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending our past never happened.
Not by erasing every earthly consequence.
But by giving repentant sinners a new standing before God and a new life in Christ.
And perhaps the most astonishing thing about this whole discussion is that the question began with the word “greater.”
We wanted to know who was greater.
We wanted to understand status, authority, and divine identity.
And Scripture led us to the cross.
To the place where the eternal Son humbled Himself.
To the place where the innocent suffered for the guilty.
To the place where our pride is exposed and God's mercy is displayed.
So when someone asks you, “If Jesus is God, why did He say the Father is greater than He is?” you do not need to panic.
You can open the Scriptures.
You can explain that John 1:1 affirms the deity of the eternal Word.
You can show that John 1:14 reveals the Word becoming flesh.
You can explain that Philippians 2 describes Christ's voluntary humiliation, not the loss of His divine nature.
You can read John 14:28 in its setting, where Jesus comforts His disciples as He prepares to return to the Father.
And you can show that the Father and Son are personally distinct without treating the Son as a created or inferior god.
But do not stop at explaining the doctrine.
Let the doctrine lead you to worship.
Because the question is not only whether you can defend the deity of Jesus.
The question is whether you have bowed before Him as Lord.
Have you trusted the Savior you claim to understand?
Have you repented of the sins you keep excusing?
Have you allowed His humility to confront your pride?
Have you received the forgiveness you cannot earn?
The Gospel does not invite you merely to admire Jesus from a distance.
It calls you to turn from sin and trust Him.
And if you have wandered, it calls you to return.
Not because you can repair your soul through religious effort.
But because the crucified and risen Christ is sufficient to save.
If these words have challenged something hidden in your heart, you do not have to pretend.
You can begin with a simple prayer:

“Lord Jesus, You are more glorious than I have understood and more merciful than I deserve. Forgive my pride, my unbelief, and my sin. Teach me to trust Your Word, surrender to Your lordship, and walk in the humility You have shown. Thank You for the cross and the hope of Your resurrection. Change my heart, and help me live for Your glory. Amen.”
And if this article has helped you understand something you once struggled to believe, I would genuinely love to hear from you.
Or tell us which verse changed the way you understand this question.
Perhaps you still have questions. You are welcome to ask them respectfully. Serious questions about Scripture deserve careful, patient answers, not ridicule.
And if you are carrying a spiritual struggle you have been afraid to admit, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
There are seasons when even those who love Jesus need encouragement from the family of faith.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to win an argument at their expense.
But to help them encounter the full witness of Scripture.
If you believe Gospel-centered teaching like this should continue reaching more people, I also want to invite you into something beyond a single article.
Gospel Warrior exists to help people encounter Jesus Christ through Scripture, understand the Gospel more deeply, grow in discipleship, and find encouragement to remain faithful.
We want these resources to remain accessible, including to people who may never be able to afford Christian books or paid study materials.

Following Gospel Warrior helps you stay connected to ongoing biblical teaching, encouragement, and discipleship resources. Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, curious seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along and examine the Scriptures for themselves.
But I want to be biblically clear about something important.
Your salvation cannot be purchased.
God's favor is not for sale.
And supporting an online ministry should never replace your responsibilities to your local church, your family, or those in genuine need.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV

The New Testament encourages believers to support those who faithfully teach the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14), but it also calls for generosity that is willing, sincere, and free from coercion.
Think of it as a recurring ministry contribution rather than a compulsory tithe. You may choose to include it in your personal giving as your convictions and circumstances allow.
You are still welcome here.
Read the free resources.
Grow in the Word.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Your worth before God is not measured by your ability to contribute financially.
What matters most is that Christ is proclaimed faithfully and that people are directed toward Him.
Because the goal has never been to build a community that simply admires Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to help build up disciples who know, love, worship, and follow Jesus Christ.
The same Jesus who was with God in the beginning.
The same Jesus who is God.
The same Jesus who became flesh.
The same Jesus who took the form of a servant.
The same Jesus who humbled Himself to death on a cross.
The same Jesus whom the Father highly exalted.
The same Jesus before whom every knee will one day bow.
And the same Jesus who still calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His finished work.
So the next time you hear someone say, “Jesus cannot be God because He said the Father is greater,” remember the whole story.
Remember the upper room.
Remember the incarnation.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember the glory He shared with the Father before the world existed.
And remember that His humility did not make Him less worthy of worship.
It revealed the astonishing depth of His love.
He did not have to stop being God to come down to us. He came down because we could never save ourselves.
